title: Alone in the Dark
shortDescription: Frédérick Raynal's Lovecraftian haunted mansion pioneer that established fixed-camera angles over pre-rendered backgrounds, founding the survival horror genre.
historicalSignificance: The grandfather of survival horror, pioneering real-time 3D polygonal characters over fixed cinematic camera backgrounds and directly inspiring Shinji Mikami's Resident Evil.

editorialContent.overview: Created in France by visionary programmer Frédérick Raynal with artist Didier Chanfray at Infogrames in late 1992, Alone in the Dark founded modern survival horror. Immersing players in the atmospheric 1920s Lovecraftian haunted mansion of Derceto in Louisiana, it proved that 3D polygonal gaming could deliver suffocating dread and cinematic cinematic pacing.
editorialContent.gameplayMechanics: Players choose to investigate Derceto as private detective Edward Carnby or artist Emily Hartwood. Trapped inside the cursed mansion, players must solve esoteric environmental puzzles, read occult journals, manage scarce revolver ammunition, and evade or defeat eldritch abominations. The game introduced deliberate 'tank controls', where directional inputs turn and propel the character relative to their own body orientation.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Raynal's stroke of genius was combining real-time 3D flat-shaded polygonal characters with static, pre-rendered 2D background illustrations viewed from fixed dramatic camera angles. By offloading complex environment geometry to pre-rendered bitmap paintings, Raynal was able to render fully articulated 3D character models on consumer 386 and 486 PCs without specialized 3D accelerator cards.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: Alone in the Dark won European game of the year accolades and established the exact mechanical and visual paradigm—fixed camera angles, limited inventory slots, pre-rendered backgrounds, and tank controls—that Shinji Mikami famously adopted and popularized worldwide in Capcom's 1996 masterpiece Resident Evil.
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Preserved on original MS-DOS floppy disk and CD-ROM releases. Emulation requires cycle-accurate x86 DOS execution and proper Sound Blaster / Roland MT-32 configuration.
